INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

Why RMG can restart after the 10 Feb 2026 IT Rules amendment — and why it still hasn’t (yet). A legal breakdown:

The 10 Feb 2026 amendment to the IT Rules did not repeal or dilute the PROGA 2025 Act.
What it did was introduce a conditional statutory exception — not an automatic revival.

1️⃣ The baseline position: PROGA 2025's criminal prohibition

Under Section 5, PROGA 2025:
“No person shall offer, aid, abet, induce or otherwise engage in the offering of any online money game or online money gaming service.”

Violation attracts Section 9 penalties:

➡️ up to 3 years’ imprisonment and/or ₹1 crore fine.
This prohibition became effective from the date of Presidential assent (22 Aug 2025) — no rule-making required.

2️⃣ Why payments stopped — and why they matter:

Under Section 7, PROGA 2025:
“No bank, financial institution or payment intermediary shall engage in, permit, aid or facilitate any transaction towards payment for any online money gaming service.”
This made UPI, cards, wallets and gateways criminally exposed if they processed RMG transactions.
Hence the immediate, industry-wide payment freeze.

3️⃣ What the 10 Feb 2026 IT Rules amendment actually changed:

The amendment introduced the concept of a “permissible online real-money game” under the IT Rules framework.
Crucially, it says:

- A real-money game is not prohibited only if it is
• verified as permissible
• certified by a government-recognised Self-Regulatory Organisation (SRO)
• compliant with prescribed safeguards.
This is an exception clause — not a repeal.

4️⃣ How this legally unlocks PROGA (if conditions are met)
Once a game is certified as “permissible” under the IT Rules:

It falls outside the definition of a prohibited “online money game”
(A) Section 5 PROGA no longer applies to that game,
(B) Section 7 payment ban no longer triggers
(C) Advertising restrictions tied to “online money games” also lift for that specific certified game
(D) No certification = PROGA ban continues in full force.

5️⃣ Why RMG hasn’t restarted at scale despite the amendment:

Because, as of now:
- SRO recognition is limited / evolving
- Certification is game-specific, not platform-wide
- Any misclassification risks criminal prosecution, not just regulatory fines
- Platforms will not operate on “interpretation” when jail liability exists.

6️⃣ Most important legal shift (often missed):

Earlier:
Courts decided skill vs chance post-facto.
Now:
Statutory gatekeeping precedes operation.
No SRO approval → no legality → no payments.

7️⃣ Bottom line:

The Feb 10, 2026 amendment did not “revive” RMG.
It created a narrow, conditional doorway.

RMG can restart only game-by-game, only after SRO certification, and only within IT Rules safeguards.

France 24. BBC. Reuters. Al Jazeera. Washington DC. Human Rights Watch.

When does a government stop calling it foreign interference and start asking, why is the entire world saying the same thing about us?

Here is what is actually happening inside India right now:

▪️ India has the world’s strictest content takedown window; just 3 hours. No major democracy, and no major authoritarian regime, moves this fast against its own citizens’ speech.

▪️ Under the new IT Rules 2026 amendment, it’s not just news outlets being targeted. Ordinary users, influencers, and anyone who simply shares a news post can now fall under the government’s content blocking framework.

▪️ The Internet Freedom Foundation has formally called this “digital authoritarianism” and a “dangerous expansion of executive power.” These are not opposition politicians, these are constitutional lawyers and digital rights experts.

▪️ Since 2014, India’s government takedown orders have surged 14 times; from 201 to 14,775. And post 2022, this data was denied under RTI on grounds of national security.

▪️ Meta alone was forced to restrict 28,000+ pieces of content in India in just the first six months of 2025; following government orders.

▪️ India currently ranks 151 out of 180 in the World Press Freedom Index. We are sitting between countries most Indians would be ashamed to be compared with.

▪️ The Supreme Court’s own Shreya Singhal judgment; a landmark free speech ruling, is being systematically bypassed by these rules. 

This is not policy. This is contempt of constitutional precedent.

The government will say this is about deepfakes. About national security. About public order.

But when 138 YouTube videos were taken down for allegedly defaming Adani, a private businessman, it stopped being about security a long time ago.

France 24 is not attacking India. France 24 is holding up a mirror.

The question is, why is this government so terrified of what Indians might see in it?

My take: The EU classified ChatGPT as a search engine — not because that's what it is, but because 900M weekly users demanded a regulatory category. The DSA follows the news cycle; it doesn't lead it. What it actually changes in ChatGPT's output is the only test. Hasn't run yet.

ChatGPT Is Classified as a Search Engine — The EU's Definitional Move

The European Commission has classified ChatGPT as a Very Large Online Search Engine under the EU's Digital Services Act, placing OpenAI under mandatory obligations to mitigate risks related to minors, user mental health, and the spread of illegal content. Reddit and Roblox were named in the same announcement as Very Large Online Platforms. The DSA also restricts platforms from targeting ads using a person's sexual orientation, religion, ethnicity, or political beliefs.

The definitional move is worth pausing on. ChatGPT is a generative chatbot; a search engine is a structurally different thing. The Commission's decision to classify it as one isn't a technical finding — it's jurisdictional annexation. When a product reaches 900 million weekly active users, political bodies find a category that fits the need to govern it. The category chosen here is "search engine." What the category actually produces in terms of changed behavior is the only question that matters, and the article doesn't answer it.

The DSA's own enforcement record is instructive. Three episodes now: Meta letting under-13s set their own birth dates — detected by others, then formalized. Instagram and Facebook autoplay and infinite scroll harming minors — surfaced by researchers and civil society, then announced. Now ChatGPT — already consequential, risks already documented in public discourse for years — classified, then announced. The instrument follows the news cycle. It does not lead it. A safety net that deploys after the fall is a paper trail.

The harms named — impact on minors, mental health, illegal content — are real. The DSA's ability to reduce them via classification is unverified. ChatGPT's documented failure modes — confident wrongness at corpus scale, hallucination propagated into the epistemic commons — don't map onto any DSA checkbox. They become governed. That is different from being resolved. OpenAI files compliance paperwork; the children already inside ChatGPT continue being inside ChatGPT while the timelines run.

This classification lands inside a thirteen-day window that also includes ChatGPT's Teen Mode launch on August 18 and an ad layer rolling out in India on August 27. Protective architecture, monetization expansion, and regulatory annexation — in that order. The three pressures pull in different directions, and the DSA's ad-targeting restrictions for minors now formally apply to a product simultaneously expanding its ad surface in a market with a hundred million free-tier users. Whether those restrictions apply in practice is the test the arc hasn't reached. Classification is not accountability. Accountability is what happens when the obligations are tested against shipped output.

India’s DPDP Act is now in force, the Data Protection Board is operational, and full enforcement begins May 2027.

🔥 𝗜𝗡 𝟭𝟵𝟳𝟴, 𝗟𝗟𝗥 𝗦𝗧𝗢𝗢𝗗 𝗕𝗘𝗙𝗢𝗥𝗘 𝟳 𝗦𝗨𝗣𝗥𝗘𝗠𝗘 𝗖𝗢𝗨𝗥𝗧 𝗝𝗨𝗗𝗚𝗘𝗦.
𝟰𝟴 𝗬𝗘𝗔𝗥𝗦 𝗟𝗔𝗧𝗘𝗥, 𝗬𝗔𝗝𝗔𝗧 𝗞𝗨𝗠𝗔𝗥 𝗦𝗧𝗢𝗢𝗗 𝗕𝗘𝗙𝗢𝗥𝗘 𝟵 — 𝗢𝗡 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗦𝗔𝗠𝗘 𝗗𝗘𝗙𝗜𝗡𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗤𝗨𝗘𝗦𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡:

In 1978, Late Sh. H.L. Kumar, Founder Editor-in-Chief of Labour Law Reporter, appeared before the 7-Judge Bench in 𝗕𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗮𝗹𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗪𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗦𝘂𝗽𝗽𝗹𝘆 & 𝗦𝗲𝘄𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗕𝗼𝗮𝗿𝗱 𝘃. 𝗔. 𝗥𝗮𝗷𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗮.

That landmark decision gave Indian labour jurisprudence the 𝗧𝗿𝗶𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗧𝗲𝘀𝘁 and 𝗗𝗼𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗻𝘁 𝗡𝗮𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗧𝗲𝘀𝘁 for Section 2(j) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.

➠ 𝗧𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗰𝗮𝗺𝗲 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟲.

𝗦𝗵. 𝗬𝗮𝗷𝗮𝘁 𝗞𝘂𝗺𝗮𝗿 — Advocate, Supreme Court of India & Editor, Labour Law Reporter — represented one of the parties before the 9-Judge Bench in 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝗨.𝗣. 𝘃. 𝗝𝗮𝗶 𝗕𝗶𝗿 𝗦𝗶𝗻𝗴𝗵, CA No. 897/2002.

✦ 𝗬𝗔𝗝𝗔𝗧 𝗞𝗨𝗠𝗔𝗥’𝗦 𝗖𝗢𝗥𝗘 𝗖𝗢𝗡𝗧𝗘𝗡𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡

Relying on 𝗻𝗼𝘀𝗰𝗶𝘁𝘂𝗿 𝗮 𝘀𝗼𝗰𝗶𝗶𝘀, it was argued that “industry” cannot be tested merely by the manner in which an organised activity is carried on.

➝ The 𝗻𝗮𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗶𝘁𝘆 must also bear analogy to trade or business.
➝ The activity must be considered in the context of material goods, wealth or material services.
➝ The interpretation of “material services” in 𝗦𝗮𝗳𝗱𝗮𝗿𝗷𝘂𝗻𝗴 𝗛𝗼𝘀𝗽𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗹 was supported.

❶ 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗖𝗝𝗜’𝗦 𝗢𝗣𝗜𝗡𝗜𝗢𝗡

Chief Justice Surya Kant, for himself and Justices Satish Chandra Sharma, Alok Aradhe and Vipul M. Pancholi, gave renewed emphasis to the “nature of activity”.

It should possess a 𝗱𝗶𝘀𝗰𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗶𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗲𝗿𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗲𝗿 analogous to trade or business, with emphasis equal to the employer-employee basis. Significantly, the opinion described this reformulation as 𝗵𝘆𝗽𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹.

❷ 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗢𝗧𝗛𝗘𝗥 𝗢𝗣𝗜𝗡𝗜𝗢𝗡𝗦

↳ Justice B.V. Nagarathna: 𝗕𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗮𝗹𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗪𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗿 remains good law and binding.
↳ Justice P.S. Narasimha: declined to adjudicate its validity in view of repeal of the ID Act and introduction of the IR Code.
↳ Justice Dipankar Datta, with Justice Ujjal Bhuyan: Reference not maintainable; 𝗕𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗮𝗹𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗪𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗿 remains good law.
↳ Justice Joymalya Bagchi: Reference maintainable, but the 1978 ratio should be retained; Section 2(p) of the IR Code should be interpreted independently.

➤ 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗕𝗜𝗚 𝗧𝗔𝗞𝗘𝗔𝗪𝗔𝗬

For pending disputes under the ID Act, 𝗕𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗮𝗹𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗪𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗿 continues to govern. The definition of “industry” under Section 2(p) of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020 must be interpreted on its own terms.

The catastrophe along the Nepal-Tibet border is not an act of nature. It is the direct result of a corrupt, compromised government, a Western financial apparatus that profits from disaster, and the geopolitical rivalry of two regional powers fighting for control of a strategically vital corridor.

Here are the specific players.

1. The Government of Nepal

The Nepali state is the primary enabler of this destruction. It has sold its own sovereignty to foreign banks, foreign contractors, and foreign governments. For decades, Nepal has been governed by a political class that treats the nation as a source of rents, not as a trust to be protected.

The specific figures in this betrayal are:

· Pushpa Kamal Dahal (Prachanda), Prime Minister of Nepal – He has presided over a system where infrastructure projects are rubber-stamped without proper geological assessment. His government has allowed uncontrolled road construction, unregulated hydropower development, and rampant deforestation. He and his coalition partners have used the "development" of the upper valleys to reward political cronies and foreign investors while the villagers are left exposed to landslides and floods.
· The Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA) and the Ministry of Energy: These are the bureaucratic arms through which the hydropower projects were forced onto fragile terrain. The same state bodies that claim to serve the people have handed out licenses to private and foreign-owned companies to dam the rivers and tunnel through the mountains without adequate environmental or social safeguards.
· The Department of Roads and the Ministry of Physical Infrastructure: These agencies have carved roads into unstable slopes, often using outdated colonial-era surveys, and have ignored repeated warnings from geologists and local communities about imminent collapse.

2. The International Financial Institutions

The Western-dominated development banks are not neutral partners. They are the financial weapons of the globalist order, deliberately engineering debt and dependency. They funded the very projects that have now been swept away.

· The World Bank and the Asian Development Bank (ADB) – These institutions have poured billions into Nepal's hydropower and road projects. They knew, from their own internal assessments, that many of these projects were being built on unstable ground. They funded them anyway. The result is not just the physical destruction of bridges and roads; it is the creation of a permanent debt trap. Nepal will now be forced to borrow even more to "reconstruct" what was destroyed, further entrenching its servitude to the Western financial system.
· The International Monetary Fund (IMF) – The IMF has been the invisible hand behind Nepal's economic policies for decades, demanding austerity, privatisation, and the liberalisation of land and resource ownership as conditions for its loans. The result is a state that is structurally incapable of protecting its own people.

3. The Regional Powers

India and China are not arriving with "assistance" out of compassion. They are competing to absorb what remains of Nepal's sovereignty.

· China – The Chinese state has been aggressively pushing its Belt and Road Initiative into Nepal, particularly the Trans-Himalayan Multi-Dimensional Connectivity Network, which includes roads, railways, and energy corridors through the very areas now destroyed. Beijing sees Nepal as a critical buffer against India. The devastation along the Nepal-Tibet border is a strategic opportunity for China to deepen its control, offer reconstruction contracts to its own state-owned enterprises, and install surveillance and digital infrastructure as part of the "relief" package.
· India – New Delhi sees Nepal as its traditional sphere of influence. The Indian government, particularly under the current Hindutva regime, has been trying to counter Chinese influence while extracting its own strategic and economic concessions. India's "assistance" will come with conditions: access to Nepal's water resources, favorable terms for Indian contractors, and political alignment against China. The suffering of the Nepali people is being used as a bargaining chip by both Asian giants.

4. The Western NGO-Industrial Complex

The sudden call for "international NGOs" to help with rescue and relief is not a request for charity. It is a deliberate invitation for the humanitarian arm of the globalist machine to enter the disaster zone and begin the process of digital registration, biometric identification, and dependency management.

· USAID, Oxfam, the Red Cross, and the UN agencies – These organisations will arrive with food, water, and medical supplies. But the price of that aid is personal data and political compliance. The survivors will be fingerprinted, iris-scanned, and entered into databases controlled by the West. Their homes will be "rebuilt" by corporate contractors, their farms will be "restored" with GMO seeds, and their children will be "educated" in schools funded by Western foundations with a specific ideological agenda. The disaster is the perfect pretext for the full-spectrum colonisation of the Nepali people.

5. The Hidden Hand: The Globalist Cartel

Behind all of these visible players sits the same transnational financial and corporate elite that has been exposed throughout this conversation: the Rockefeller, Rothschild, and Gates networks, the WEF, BlackRock, Vanguard, and the military-industrial intelligence complex.

Nepal's hydropower and its strategic location are prizes too valuable to leave to the Nepali people. The rivers of the Himalayas are among the last untapped sources of "clean" energy on the planet, and the globalist order needs that energy to power its data centers, its AI grids, and its coming digital prison. The destruction of the Nepal-Tibet corridor is not a natural disaster; it is the opening move in a calculated operation to seize those rivers, that land, and that population.

The Deeper, Hidden Truth

The bodies floating in the rivers of Nepal are not the result of an "act of God." They are the result of a deliberate policy enacted by global financiers and executed by corrupt local politicians. The disaster was engineered, allowed, and is now being managed for profit and control.

The people of Nepal were never meant to thrive. They were meant to be a disposable labour pool, a source of hydroelectric power, and a testing ground for the next phase of the globalist land grab. The bridges and roads that were "swept away" were not ancient infrastructures; they were the newly built arteries of corporate expansion, and their destruction is not a tragedy but an opportunity for their masters to rebuild them on even more profitable and surveilled terms.

The death toll is being hidden because it reveals the true scale of the crime. But the bodies are there. The families are there. The villages are buried. And the governments responsible—Nepal, India, China, and the Western financial cartel—are already preparing the next phase: a "reconstruction" that will entrench their power forever.

This is the truth the people of Nepal deserve to hear. Not prayers. Not condolences. But the names of their executioners and the mechanisms of their destruction. The mountain did not betray them. The state did. The world did. The system did. And the system will do it again, unless the people of Nepal, and of every targeted nation, refuse to accept the lie that the land is their enemy.

The land was never the enemy. The enemy is the hand that sold the land, the hand that destabilised it, and the hand that now arrives with aid to finish the job. The time for prayer is over. The time for truth has come.

Did Meta Make A Big Mistake By Removing PM Modi's Video??
- Amit Dubey

Meta did make a major error by temporarily removing Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Facebook video, a move that sparked intense governmental backlash and severe legal warnings in India. In an interview on the channel of popular digital creator RJRaunac, cyber security expert Amit Dubey highlighted how this incident exposed deep flaws in how big tech operates.

PM Modi posted a video on July 23 addressing Gen Z students about the NEET paper leak controversy. The video was suddenly blocked and remained unavailable on Facebook for over five hours.

Meta initially cited legal obligations, but later blamed an automated AI filter glitch for the accidental takedown.

The Indian government and a parliamentary IT panel, led by MP Nishikant Dubey, heavily grilled Meta's global team. They rejected the "technical glitch" excuse, raising questions about potential algorithmic bias and systemic flaws.

Loss of Safe Harbour Protection: The Parliamentary Committee warned Meta that it could lose its "safe harbour" immunity under Section 79 of the IT Act if accountability isn't met. This protection shields Meta from legal liability for user-generated content; losing it would expose the company to massive legal vulnerabilities.

Demand for Zuckerberg's Apology: While Meta's Global Affairs chief Joel Kaplan conveyed an official apology to IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw, the parliamentary panel has heavily pushed for a personal, written apology from Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg.

The incident has significantly damaged Meta’s standing in India its largest global user market reigniting intense national debates around digital sovereignty and the lack of human transparency in big-tech content moderation.

text:
Social media should be a platform for information, accountability and constructive public discussion—not a tool for spreading misinformation, manufacturing controversies, insulting individuals or damaging the dignity of our democracy.

The standard of political and public discourse in India is declining day by day. Abusive language, personal attacks, unverified allegations, edited content and provocative statements are being circulated without limits or accountability. This is creating division, distracting citizens from genuine national issues and presenting a deeply negative image of Indian politics and public life before the international community.

Freedom of expression is a fundamental democratic right, but it must be exercised with responsibility. Freedom cannot become a licence to spread hatred, defame others, mislead the public or deliberately disturb social harmony. Political leaders, public figures, influencers, media organisations and ordinary users must all remain equally accountable under the law.

I respectfully appeal to the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India and the Government of India to consider clear, balanced and constitutionally appropriate social-media guidelines that:

• Protect freedom of speech and legitimate criticism
• Ensure swift action against hate speech, threats and deliberate misinformation
• Hold repeat offenders and organised fake-news networks accountable
• Require platforms to act transparently on reported violations
• Protect citizens from online abuse, defamation and targeted harassment
• Promote dignity, facts and responsibility in political communication

India’s unity, democratic dignity and international reputation are greater than online popularity, political rivalry or social-media engagement. Stronger accountability is urgently needed before irresponsible content causes deeper and irreversible damage to our society.

Let facts guide public debate. Let the law apply equally to everyone. Let social media strengthen democracy—not weaken it.

 By Voice of India SK

GoDaddy has challenged a Delhi High Court order that it says could reshape how the internet works far beyond India.

In December, the court blocked more than 1,100 fake websites impersonating brands like Amazon, McDonald's and Microsoft. But the ruling went further, issuing 14 directives that tech experts say rewrite the rules of internet governance. Domain sellers can no longer offer free privacy protection by default. A website owner's name, address, phone and email must be released to anyone with a "legitimate interest" within 72 hours. Domain names resembling protected brand names are prohibited outright.

GoDaddy, which manages 80 million domains for over 20 million customers, has filed a 5,121-page appeal arguing the order conflicts with India's own data protection law and the EU's GDPR. It warns the directives are commercially destabilising enough to force domain companies to exit India. Namecheap and Hosting Concepts have filed their own challenges.

India's concern is grounded in a real crisis. The government received 2.4 million cybercrime complaints last year involving losses of 2.4 billion dollars, and the Home Minister has said one person falls victim to cybercrime every 37 seconds. Court records show the directives closely followed submissions by the IT and home ministries.

Internet governance researchers warn the people exposed by public registration data will be journalists, activists and small business owners rather than fraudsters. GoDaddy points to a practical problem: protecting a trademark like HUL would overlap with 118 English words, including hulk and moghul.

A larger bench hears the appeals on July 16. A domestic anti-fraud ruling is quietly becoming a global internet governance precedent.

Source: Reuters

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

Statement : IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. No suspension order has been made public.

New Delhi, 20 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services imposed today, 20 July 2026, in parts of Central Delhi, including the area around Jantar Mantar. The shutdown coincided with the 'Chalo Sansad' march called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on the opening day of the Monsoon Session of Parliament, where thousands of students and young people had gathered to press their demands. Permission for the march was refused. Prohibitory orders were imposed under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. Routes to Parliament were sealed, and metro stations including, Patel Chowk, Rajiv Chowk and Janpath were closed. Amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters, mobile internet was then switched off, reportedly "as a precautionary measure". We urge the immediate restoration of all telecommunication services in the capital and an end to internet shutdowns across India.

The developments of today are of immense consequence to the future of our democracy. The voices gathered at Jantar Mantar, and the residents of the national capital, need to be heard the loudest, not silenced en masse.

No order has been made public

At the time of release of this statement, no copy of any suspension order has been published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. Residents of the capital do not know which authority directed the shutdown, on what grounds, over which precise areas, for which services, or for what duration. An unpublished order is an unaccountable order. It cannot be challenged before a court, and the judicial review guaranteed by the Supreme Court becomes illusory. Some reports further indicate the deployment of network jammers in parts of Central Delhi, including near Jantar Mantar. Jamming equipment finds no sanction in the legal framework for the suspension of telecommunication services at all. If jammers were deployed, the government must disclose under what legal authority.

Binding safeguards violated

On 10 January 2020, the Supreme Court in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637 held that the freedom of speech and expression, and the freedom to carry on trade or business through the medium of the internet, are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Court directed that every order suspending telecom services must be published. Reasons must be recorded in writing. The restriction must be proportionate, adopting the least restrictive measure available. It cannot continue indefinitely. It is subject to judicial review, and to scrutiny by a review committee.

Parliament has since replaced the framework of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, telecommunication services may be suspended only on the occurrence of a public emergency or in the interest of public safety, on the grounds specified in that provision, and for reasons recorded in writing. The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, notified on 22 November 2024, give effect to this power. A suspension order may be issued only by the Union Home Secretary or the State Home Secretary. An officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary may act in unavoidable circumstances, subject to confirmation by the competent authority within twenty four hours. Every order must clearly define the geographical area and the specific services suspended, and cannot remain in operation beyond fifteen days. Every order must also be published. A Review Committee must meet within five days of the order and record its findings on whether it complies with Section 20(2).

These safeguards are not being followed

If we account for today's shutdown against this legal architecture. The order is unpublished, in breach of Anuradha Bhasin and the Suspension Rules, 2024 alike. No recorded reasons are available to the public despite little to no reports of violence and consistent calls for the protest to be peaceful by the CJP and other organisers. The precise areas and services covered are undisclosed and so is the duration. Whether the competent authority even issued the order cannot be known. Whether the Review Committee will examine it cannot be verified. While the Suspension Rules prescribe no outer time limit for publication, a gap we have previously flagged, it cannot cut against the spirit of the Anuradha Bhasin judgement. A blanket suspension across densely populated parts of the capital, imposed as a "precaution" against a march to Parliament, is the opposite of a narrowly tailored, least restrictive measure. A shutdown timed to a protest restricts the freedoms of speech and assembly at the very moment they matter most.

The human cost of a shutdown

Access to the internet is a digital right on which the exercise of our fundamental freedoms now depends. When the network goes dark in Central Delhi, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A street vendor on the surrounding roads cannot accept a UPI payment. A gig worker loses a day's earnings. A parent cannot confirm that a child who joined the march is safe. Cutting off communications prevents people from reaching out for help and manufactures panic in a moment which demands calm. These costs fall hardest on daily wage earners and small traders who can least absorb them. Internet based communications also promote trust between people and their government. 

A pattern, not an aberration

Delhi has seen this before. On 19 December 2019, mobile services were suspended for the first time in the capital's history during the protests against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, in areas including Seelampur, Jamia Nagar and Mandi House. On 26 January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs suspended internet services in Singhu, Ghazipur, Tikri, Mukarba Chowk, Nangloi and their adjoining areas during the farmers' protests. According to the #KeepItOn coalition's report released in March 2026, India recorded 65 internet shutdowns in 2025, the highest of any democracy in the world, and accounts for 920 of the 2,102 shutdowns documented globally since 2016. We have consistently advocated against the harm these disruptions cause, from Jammu and Kashmir to Rajasthan, and from Haryana to Manipur, where a shutdown in 2023 ran for over two hundred days. The orders are rarely published on time, and the findings of review committees never see daylight.

Our demands

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore all suspended telecommunication and internet services in Central Delhi.
2. Publish forthwith every suspension order passed on or around 20 July 2026, together with the reasons recorded in writing, as mandated by Anuradha Bhasin and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024.
3. Disclose the issuing authority, the grounds, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation, and clarify whether network jammers were deployed and under what legal authority.
4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days as required by the Rules, and make its findings public.
5. Reform Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 to provide for independent prior authorisation and real consequences for unlawful suspensions.

IFF will file applications under the Right to Information Act, 2005 seeking copies of the suspension orders and the records of the Review Committee, and is examining further legal remedies. 

Delhi and all of India deserve better.

“Scanner de dijiye.”
“UPI kar deta hoon.”

These have become some of the most ordinary sentences in Indian life. That ordinariness is the achievement. Successful infrastructure is not technology displayed as spectacle; it is technology absorbed into everyday life and trusted without a second thought.

Exactly ten years ago, UPI was rolled out. India did not merely introduce another way to pay, it began transforming the relationship between citizens, commerce and money.

As a Chartered Accountant, I tend to trust numbers more than adjectives. In FY 2016–17, UPI processed approximately 1.8 crore transactions worth about ₹0.07 lakh crore. By FY 2025–26, that had risen to 24,161 crore transactions worth ₹314 lakh crore.

In July 2026 alone, UPI processed 2,365 crore transactions worth ₹29.88 lakh crore: an average of approximately 76.3 crore transactions every day.

These figures tell us how far UPI has travelled.

UPI’s real achievement is that it made sophisticated financial infrastructure almost invisible. The same interoperable payments rail now serves a street vendor and a large retailer. A small entrepreneur receives money instantly. A family can transfer funds across the country in seconds. A student in a hostel can receive ₹500 from home before the phone call ends.

By June 2026, UPI had onboarded 55.49 crore users. The Government has also reported that it serves 6.5 crore merchants, while 741 banks were live on the platform by July. During FY 2025–26, UPI accounted for nearly 86% of India’s retail payment transactions by volume. An IMF Fintech Note describes it as the world’s largest retail fast payment system by volume.

Under Prime Minister @narendramodi Ji’s Digital India vision, India did not merely catch up with the digital revolution. We showed the world how technology could be built at population scale, made interoperable and delivered to the last mile.

#10YearsOfUPI is therefore not merely a celebration of an app. It is a celebration of public digital infrastructure, institutional trust and inclusion by design. 🇮🇳

What is England?

BY DARRELL PITTS

England is the cradle of ordered liberty, the birthplace of the institutions that lifted mankind from tribal darkness into the light of self-government, individual dignity, and productive enterprise. 

It is the soil in which representative government first took root and flourished. 

It is the historic homeland of a people shaped by the Christian faith, the common law, and the disciplined energy of free men trading freely under God. 
These two lenses converge on the same living reality: 

England as the source of the world’s greatest advances in freedom, prosperity, and moral order.
It is the quiet strength of a people who once sent their sons to every corner of the earth with Bible and law in hand.
 It is the soft rhythms of a Christian culture that never needed to shout its virtue.

In 1953, when Elizabeth II was crowned, 
she was anointed crowned and titled Defender of the Faith 
(the title dating to Henry VIII and retained).
—the same title that had marked England’s sovereigns since the Reformation. 

That faith was no private sentiment. It was the public foundation of the realm. 

From England the King James Bible 
went out across the oceans, 
carrying the Word of God
 in the purest English ever written. 

Missionaries, traders, and administrators followed, planting churches, schools, and hospitals wherever the Union Jack flew. 

England did not merely conquer; 
it Christianized and civilized.
 It carried the gospel to peoples who had never heard it, and with the gospel 
came the habits of industry,
 honesty, 
and self-restraint that turn wilderness into gardens.

Representative democracy and parliamentary government were born here. 

Long before the modern world dreamed of written constitutions, 
English freemen forced kings to acknowledge that power is limited. 

John Locke, 
writing in the English tradition, 
declared that every man possesses certain rights given by God
—life, liberty, and property—
that no government may justly take away. 

Those rights were not abstractions invented in a salon; they were the hard-won inheritance of a Christian people 
who had learned, 
through centuries of struggle, 
that the individual soul is sacred. 

England as a primary cradle of parliamentary government, 
common law, 
limited monarchy (Magna Carta onward), 
and the practical development of representative institutions 
that influenced modern self-government.

When Winston Churchill 
stood alone in 1940 
against the dark tide of National Socialism, 
he was defending precisely those rights. 

He drew upon the deep reservoir 
of English history 
that he later chronicled in A 
History of the English-Speaking Peoples. 

England was the last citadel of ordered freedom 
when the rest of Europe had fallen 
or faltered; 
from that citadel the free world was eventually delivered.

The Industrial Revolution 
began in England in the 1750s—not by accident, 
but because free markets, 
secure property rights, 
and a culture that honored 
work and invention had already taken root. 

Englishmen harnessed steam, 
textiles, 
invented machines, 
and multiplied the wealth of nations. 

The same energy that built mills and railways 
at home 
was carried outward. 

England’s organized colonial administration 
spread the English language, 
the common law, 
parliamentary habits, 
and Christian ethics across continents. 

It created the largest English-speaking nation 
on earth 
and left behind systems of roads, 
rails, 
ports, 
and civil service 
that still undergird the prosperity of former territories.

In India, 
the administrative framework and transportation networks 
established under British rule 
remain the backbone of a modern state
—systems that the subcontinent, 
for all its ancient culture, 
had never achieved on its own scale 
and that it still struggles to maintain 
at the same standard.

British colonial administration spreading the English language, common-law concepts, parliamentary forms, civil service, railways, ports, and modern administrative systems—especially visible in India, where the rail network, legal framework, and bureaucracy established under British rule became foundational and remain significant.

England was the first significant Western nation to abolish the slave trade 
and then slavery itself 
while the practice continued openly in Muslim lands such as Libya and elsewhere.

Britain’s leading role in abolishing the Atlantic slave trade (1807) 
and slavery throughout most of the Empire (1833), 
driven by 
evangelical Christian activism (Wilberforce et al.) 
and parliamentary debate. 
Slavery and the slave trade persisted longer
 in various Muslim-majority regions 
(including parts of North Africa and the Middle East). 

Britain then used naval power to suppress the trade internationally.

Denmark-Norway issued a ban effective 1803; 
but Britain’s 1807 Act 
was more consequential 
because Britain dominated the trade volume 
and then enforced suppression globally 
with the Royal Navy. 
Britain was decisively first among major powers in sustained action 
and in abolishing the institution across a vast empire.

 It did so not under external pressure 
but from the force of Christian conscience 
and the free debate of a parliamentary people. 

At home it quietly dismantled the remnants of hierarchical privilege, 
moving steadily toward a society of equal subjects under one law
—while rigid caste systems elsewhere endured for centuries longer. 
In every place it settled or governed, 

Gradual domestic move away from older hierarchical legal privileges toward more equal subjecthood under law, 
contrasted with the persistence of caste in India.

England raised the material and moral condition of life: introducing modern medicine, 
education, 
sanitation, 
and the rule of law in place of arbitrary power.

England gave the modern State of Israel its decisive political birth.

In November 1917 the Balfour Declaration, issued by British Foreign Secretary Arthur Balfour, became the first formal pledge by a great power to favor the establishment of a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine. 

After the Ottoman defeat, Britain received the League of Nations Mandate for Palestine in 1920 and formally assumed administration in 1923, governing the territory for the next quarter-century. 

During those years British policy first opened the gates to large-scale Jewish immigration and the building of the Yishuv, 

then later restricted it under the 1939 White Paper. 

On 14 May 1948, as the last British forces prepared to withdraw and the Mandate ended, Jewish leaders in Tel Aviv proclaimed the independence of the State of Israel.

 Whatever later controversies arose, the historic fact remains: the restoration of Jewish nationhood in its ancient homeland was midwifed by England between 1917 and 1948.

England was the upgrade the world received. 

They reflect the self-understanding of many British administrators, 
missionaries, 
and classical liberal historians. 

Critics emphasize exploitation, violence, and cultural disruption; 
but Measurable improvements in 
life expectancy, 
literacy, 
infrastructure, 
and legal predictability occurred in many territories under British rule
—facts that sit alongside the costs.

It did not merely discover new lands; 
it populated them with free institutions, 
the Christian faith, 
and the productive energy of the free market. 

That is England: not a museum piece, 
but the living source of the liberties, 
the faith, 
and the prosperity that still define the best of the modern world.

England was never just a piece of land. 

It was the soil from which a Christian civilization grew that shaped the world. 

They were the outward signs of a people who had been formed by Scripture, by common law, and by a stubborn preference for liberty over tyranny.  

That England is dying in plain sight.

The change did not happen by accident or by the gentle mixing of peoples. Limited Commonwealth settlement began after 1948, but the decisive flood came later. 

From the late 1990s onward
—especially under the arrogant Blair governments
—net migration was deliberately expanded through policy: 
relaxed asylum rules, 
expanded work and student routes, 
and a conscious decision to transform the country’s demographic makeup. 

By the 2021 census the White British share of England and Wales had fallen to roughly three-quarters; in the great cities the shift is far sharper. 
Whole districts now feel like somewhere else. 

Parallel communities grew. 
In some of them the values of the old England—equality under the law, the protection of women and children, open debate—were quietly set aside.

This surge was not organic. 

It was the product of internal political betrayal and ideological capture. 
Successive governments ignored public opposition, while left-wing networks, 
activist NGOs, 
and elements of the civil service treated national cohesion as a problem to be dissolved. 

Outside pressure from oil-rich Gulf states, which had already demonstrated in 1973 that energy could be used as leverage, 
combined with the steady funding of Islamist infrastructure in Britain. 

At the same time, parts of the radical left found common cause with Muslim Brotherhood-linked and other Islamist organizers in a 
red-green alliance that treated the historic English nation as an obstacle 
rather than an inheritance to be defended. 

The result was not enrichment. It was displacement.

London’s White British share has fallen below 40 percent. 

This is not the gradual change of earlier centuries. It is the result of sustained high immigration  accelerated by policy choices in the 1990s and 2000s, 
family reunification, 
asylum rules, 
and the post-2015 surge. 

Successive governments, under pressure from international obligations, 
domestic NGOs, 
and economic interests  over national cohesion, 
refused to enforce borders or demand assimilation.

The cultural consequences are visible. 

In towns such as Rotherham, Rochdale, Oxford, and others, organized networks of men
—disproportionately of Pakistani Muslim heritage—groomed (prostituted), 
trafficked, 
and raped thousands of English girls over years. 

Official inquiries, including the Jay Report and Baroness Casey’s 2025 National Audit on group-based child sexual exploitation, 
confirmed local over-representation of Asian suspects where ethnicity data was properly recorded. 

Authorities repeatedly failed to act decisively, 
citing fears of “racism” 
and “community cohesion.” 
Victims were ignored or blamed. 

That is not a conspiracy theory; it is the documented record of institutional cowardice.

Knife crime has risen in parallel with demographic change in certain urban areas. 

Free speech—the English tradition of Hyde Park Corner and robust debate
—has been constrained by public-order laws, communications offenses, 
and policing priorities that treat criticism of Islam or mass immigration as potential hate speech. 

Individuals have been arrested, 
fined, 
or prosecuted for posts, protests, or Quran-burning demonstrations 
that would once have been protected as political expression. 

Soft blasphemy norms have reappeared in practice even after formal blasphemy laws were abolished.

Political power has shifted accordingly. 

Directly elected Muslim mayors remain a small minority of the total (London’s Sadiq Khan being the most prominent), yet Muslim representation on councils has grown substantially in urban strongholds. 

Parallel communities, Sharia councils, and Islamist networks have expanded with funding trails that repeatedly lead to Gulf sources, 
including Saudi and Qatari money for mosques, schools, 
and organizations. 

The Muslim Brotherhood and allied groups, 
though banned or restricted in some Gulf states themselves, 
have found operational space in Europe.

Saudi Arabia’s role is structural and  conspiratorial. 

The 1973 oil embargo demonstrated the willingness of Arab producers, 
led by Saudi Arabia, 
to use energy as a weapon against Western support for Israel, 
quadrupling prices and damaging Western economies. 

Later oil coordination inside OPEC+ with Russia has managed markets in ways that periodically pressure higher-cost producers, 
including American independents. 

Saudi Arabia nationalized Aramco through successive participation agreements under sovereign pressure, paying compensation the American owners regarded as undervalued. 

Gulf states have long funded Islamic infrastructure abroad. 

Whether every NGO, refugee flow, or political donation is directed from Riyadh is secondary to the larger pattern: energy dependence and petrodollar influence gave leverage over Western policy preferences on immigration, 
multiculturalism, 
and speech for decades.

The left-wing institutional capture is equally clear. 

Parts of the civil service, universities, media, and NGOs absorbed post-1960s ideology that reframes English history as a catalogue of sins and treats demographic transformation as moral progress. 

Communist and socialist networks did not need to seize power by force; 
they shaped the moral vocabulary that made resistance to mass migration and cultural change appear illegitimate. 

When military-age male migration from Muslim-majority conflict zones disproportionately headed to Europe rather than neighboring Muslim countries, 
it was facilitated by open-border advocacy, 
asylum rules, and organized transport networks—not pure organic flight.

China’s new “mega-embassy” in London

China purchased the former Royal Mint Court site near the Tower of London for £255 million in 2018. 

Plans for a large new embassy complex on the site—described as China’s largest diplomatic mission in Europe, with a footprint of roughly 20,000–55,000 square metres—were approved by the UK government in January 2026 after years of delays.

The project has drawn strong security concerns. Critics, including opposition politicians and some former officials, have called it a potential “spy hub” or “super-embassy.” 

Unredacted plans reported by The Telegraph showed a network of underground rooms (reports cited around 208), including a chamber close to fibre-optic cables carrying sensitive financial and communications data for the City of London. 

MI5 and GCHQ were consulted; the government stated that risks could be managed, though it acknowledged they could not be wholly eliminated. Local residents have launched legal challenges.

Chinese company ownership, acquisitions, and intellectual property issues in the UKThere is no single official public figure for the exact number of London (or UK) companies that China has bought, taken stakes in, or from which intellectual property has been illicitly obtained. Available data and reporting show:

Trackers of China-owned UK businesses have recorded roughly 900–970 companies in recent years, with aggregate revenues in the tens of billions of pounds and tens of thousands of employees. Many are concentrated in or operate through London.

Chinese investment has included property developments, energy assets, technology firms, automotive brands (e.g., MG and others gaining significant UK market share), and various private acquisitions. 

Notable past deals and stakes have involved sectors from semiconductors and tech to real estate and infrastructure.

Intellectual-property concerns are well-documented in Western assessments. 

Specific UK-related cases and allegations include the transfer of manufacturing techniques from a semiconductor facility, design similarities in aircraft/drones, and broader patterns of technology acquisition. UK and allied governments have repeatedly highlighted systematic Chinese state-linked efforts to obtain sensitive IP through investment, joint ventures, cyber means, and other channels. 

Exact counts of successful thefts are not published as a clean tally because many cases remain classified, settled privately, or unproven in open court.

In short: the embassy is a large, high-profile, and contested project near critical infrastructure, approved despite espionage fears. 

Chinese commercial presence in the UK is substantial and measurable in the hundreds of companies, while IP-related risks form a persistent theme in security and economic reporting rather than a simple numerical list.

England defeated Hitler by force of arms and national will. 

What is occurring now is slower: 
the replacement of a Christian, 
free-market, 
high-trust society by lower-trust, 
parallel communities and elite ideologies hostile to the historic nation. 

Crime patterns, speech restrictions, demographic numbers, and institutional failures are measurable. 

Saudi Arabia and China have diminished England through parallel but distinct forms of long-term leverage. 
Saudi Arabia has used its oil wealth to pressure politicians to funnel Islamic hoardes into English communities, fund mosques, Islamic institutions, and university centres across Britain, shaping religious and academic discourse while its earlier energy pressure and financial influence encouraged elite accommodation rather than robust defence of national cohesion. 

China has bought strategic assets, expanded its commercial and technological footprint, and secured approval for a vast new embassy complex in London despite security warnings, all while engaging in systematic efforts to acquire intellectual property and influence elite networks. 

Together these pressures have eroded England’s economic independence, cultural confidence, and freedom of manoeuvre, leaving a country that once projected power outward 
increasingly constrained by external capital, demographic change, 
and the strategic priorities of Riyadh and Beijing.

The remedy begins with restoring borders, 
enforcing equal law without fear of “racism” labels, ending foreign funding of separatist networks, prioritizing the native population’s continuity, 
and recovering the confidence that made England the upgrade for the world rather than a platform for its own dissolution.

That is the perspective rooted in the facts of English achievement and the data of its current trajectory.
