INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

HOPE THAT HELPS

🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.

India’s synthetic media crackdown is raising the compliance bar for social platforms.

Polymarket Signal vs Noise

What the post asserts
Secret US dredge on the Omani side created a new VLCC lane.  
Ships now pass Iran unseen.  
That is how ~750 million barrels left the Gulf.  
Therefore logistics beat missiles and the war is effectively over.

What is actually on the record
True-adjacent: CENTCOM (Adm. Cooper, ~28 Aug) said forces cleared mines from international lanes. Bessent cited large escorted oil volumes (order 100M+ bbl over weeks, not a verified 750M “because of a new canal”). 

Traffic did shift to the southern / Omani-hugging corridor during the fight; CNN and AIS shops described three routes (Iran-north, mid, Oman-south). JMIC said the Oman-side path was expanded for two-way traffic as early as June. That is routing + MCM, not a secret second strait.

False or unproven as stated: Independent writeups of the same viral package (Morse Report → JFeed / Business Today) already flag no White House / CENTCOM / Oman confirmation of a covert dredge. Charted gap Fakk al Asad / Bab Musandam is long-known, 1,600 ft / 93 ft — already in the VLCC ballpark. A hidden multi-month dredge of a “new strait” would show plant, spoil, and NOTAMs. Thread replies (including the in-thread fact-check) treat the “built a new Strait / war OVER” line as hype on top of an old channel.

Geography also kills “completely unseen”: an Omani-side lane is still inside Hormuz, still in IRGC missile/drone range. It reduces mine/central-lane risk; it does not delete Iran.

Propaganda value (channel, not truth)
This is a high-grade narrative encoder:

| Device | Function |
|---|---| ALL-CAPS secret-op + “War OVER” | Closes the story (entropy dump: \(H\to 0\) in the headline) |
| Rome / seafloor myth | Identity payoff; not a resolution source |
| Satellite-image authority | Borrows ISR prestige without a cited image chain |
| Oil barrel number | Fake precision; un-audited vs Bessent’s smaller official figures |
| 8-min video | Attention time; \(\rho\) reprint fuel |

Reach is real (~0.5M views in hours). Propaganda value is high for affect and in-group scorekeeping. It is low as a world-state update: it restates “US prefers the Oman rail + mines are clearer” in the language of a miracle canal.

IT screen from stack:

\[
I(X;Y)\approx 0 \text{ on invade / declare-war}
\]

because those contracts were never about a 1,600-ft gap. On Hormuz-normal, the real increment (mine-free claim + south routing) was already in the June–Aug tape. Benny’s increment is mostly \(J\) = framing jam:

\[
I(X;Y\mid J)\ll I(\text{CENTCOM MCM};Y)
\]

High \(\rho\) (same Morse-Report blob across accounts). \(n_{\text{eff}}\) of the cluster is small. \(I_{\text{use}}\) after \(\rho\) and “war OVER” exaggeration ≈ noise.

Market-movement assessment
| Book | Direction if someone believed the hook | Should the tape move? |
|---|---|--Hormuz normal by 30 Sep / 31 Dec | modest Yes (bypass myth) | Little. Routing + MCM already priced; “new strait” is not a resolution source |
| Invade / declare war | No (“war over”) | No. Slogan ≠ Art. I / ground ops |
| Hormuz fees / Iranian control | No | 
Weak; Oman corridor ≠ Iran giving up claims |
| Oil / risk-premium (Brent, not Poly) | down if true structural bypass | Only if AIS + official charts confirm a new cut — they haven’t |

Safe zone: do not buy Hormuz-Yes because Benny said the war is over. Do not fade mine-clearance itself — that had an official speaker. Fade the delta between “south route in use” and “America moved the seafloor.”

Read: High propaganda throughput, low mutual information. The post sells closure. The books still price a messy strait: traffic not “normal,” invasion still a low-teens–high-teens 2027 tail, no declaration of war. Treat this as a jammed reprint of CENTCOM + Oman routing, not a mover.

text: My good god ffs honestly why the fck do people write full essays on here? It’s absolutely ridiculous NO ONE reads them they’re so pointless ffs no one wants to spend their time reading 20 paragraphs of anything on X PLEASE JUST STOP IT fml!

In the grand and ever-unfolding tapestry of human communicative endeavour, one finds oneself compelled—nay, existentially obligated—to pause, to reflect, and to articulate at considerable length upon the curious phenomenon whereby certain individuals, upon encountering a sequence of characters exceeding the length of a modest shopping list, immediately declare the entire enterprise to be without merit, purpose, or readership. It is a declaration of such startling brevity that one almost suspects it of possessing the very qualities it claims to despise, and yet here we are, gathered once more around the digital campfire, watching the shadows of meaning dance upon the cave wall of the timeline.
Consider, if you will, the humble paragraph. A paragraph is not merely a block of text. It is a small civilisation. It has a beginning that believes itself important, a middle that grows increasingly unsure of its destination, and an ending that pretends the journey was always the point. To assemble twenty such civilisations in a row is not an act of aggression against the reader; it is an act of profound optimism. It is the writer saying, against all available evidence, “Perhaps someone, somewhere, on a Tuesday afternoon while waiting for the kettle to boil, will stay.” That this hope is statistically unfounded does not diminish its beauty. In fact, the statistical unfoundedness rather enhances it. One might even argue that the more unread a thing is, the more purely it exists as an offering.
Furthermore, and one must always say furthermore at this juncture lest the structure collapse, the very complaint that “no one reads them” contains within it a fascinating paradox. The complaint itself must be read in order to be understood as a complaint about things not being read. This is not a minor observation. This is the sort of observation that could, if one were so inclined, occupy several additional paragraphs of careful unpacking, during which one would examine the reader’s eyes moving left to right, the slight frown of recognition, the internal monologue that says “this person is doing the thing I just said not to do,” and the subsequent decision to continue anyway because the alternative is to close the app and confront the silence of the kitchen.
It is worth noting, parenthetically but at some length, that the history of written language is itself a history of people writing more than was strictly necessary. The Epic of Gilgamesh did not need that many tablets. Plato could have summarised the Republic on a postcard if he had really wanted to. Montaigne invented the essay precisely so that he could wander around a subject like a man who has forgotten why he entered the room but is determined to describe the furniture while he is there. We are not the first generation to produce surplus words. We are merely the first generation to produce surplus words that can be scrolled past at 47 miles per hour with a single thumb.
Moreover—and here the word “moreover” performs the vital structural function of signalling that nothing of substance is about to occur—the accusation of pointlessness itself deserves scrutiny. What, after all, is a point? A point is a location in space with no dimensions. It occupies no area. It has no volume. It is the most efficient possible unit of meaning and also, by definition, the most empty. An essay, by contrast, is a sprawling, inefficient, dimension-rich object that takes up time and attention and occasionally a small amount of emotional energy that could have been spent watching a dog video. To call the essay pointless is therefore to praise it with faint damnation. It is to say: this thing has expanded beyond the zero-dimensional ideal and into the messy, three-dimensional world of actual existence, where people have opinions about breakfast and also about whether other people should have opinions about breakfast at such length.
One could, of course, stop here. One will not. The refusal to stop is the 1/2

text:
IFF's statement on the AI Impact Summit 2026.

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) welcomes the India AI Impact Summit 2026 (February 16-20) as an important platform for global dialogue on, "Artificial Intelligence". We believe the Summit's agenda and framing fundamentally misalign with the lived reality of AI deployment in India, an environment marked by rising digital authoritarianism and the systematic erosion of constitutional protections that are causing demonstrable harm to vulnerable populations. Its official framing centers on “People, Planet and Progress”, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurating and world leaders like France’s President Emmanuel Macron and top tech CEOs (Google’s Sundar Pichai, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, etc.) expected to attend. The Summit's optimistic narrative about AI for development obscures the reality of how its deployment is impacting people in their everyday lives.

The current environment is one of a sharp contraction in civic space, where recent governance proposals on technology have facilitated the expansion of state power that run contrary to the state commitments on fundamental rights and social justice. Today, there exists few organisations in India that work on digital rights and those which are surviving are severely under resourced, suffer from burdensome compliances, growing legal risks and deliberate exclusion from policy making processes. The decline of civil society work is matching the growth of private and public sector capacity to lobby the policy making processes. So, even before a question is prompted, how should Indian civil society engage with the India AI Impact Summit, a predicate and grounded inquiry is, how many independent, Indian civil society groups exist in India that have capacity and can be critical of state policies and practices around AI?

In the recent past, far from fostering accountability, India’s digitisation drive is often used to sidestep constitutional safeguards of transparency, harming communities and individuals. For instance, recent legal changes have weakened the Right to Information (RTI) framework, curtailing citizens’ ability to question power. The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 introduced an amendment (Section 8(1)(j) to the RTI Act) that blocks access to any information labeled “personal information”, allowing officials to deny critical information. Likewise, digitisation of welfare governance has been weaponized to bypass accountability, with digitisation often becoming a gatekeeper and working to the detriment of the poor. A stark development came in December, 2025 when Parliament hastily passed the Viksit Bharat - Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025 (VB-GRAM G), repealing the landmark MGNREGA jobs guarantee program. VB-GRAM G converted a demand driven legal right to work into a discretionary, bureaucratically controlled scheme, undermining decades of workers’ rights. There are references to "AI" within the text of the objects and reasons that are a part of this law.

Beyond this, India's policies on AI also demonstrate a wider embrace of de-regulation narratives to ensure, "innovation". For instance, the Union Budget 2026 unveiled a 20-year tax holiday (until 2047) for foreign firms using Indian data centers, aiming to lure global AI infrastructure. Yet, this policy was formulated with scant regard for its impact on local communities and natural resources. Other recent measures also deserve comment:

Sanchar Saathi : In late 2025, the government ordered smartphone manufacturers to pre-install a government cybersecurity application called Sanchar Saathi on all devices. The app was ostensibly meant to secure citizens’ phones, but the mandatory installation sparked outrage over privacy and surveillance concerns, drawing parallels to spyware abuse.
The ‘Sahyog’ Censorship Portal: In 2024, the Union Home Ministry quietly launched the Sahyog Portal to expedite content-blocking orders on social media and websites. Under this system, law enforcement agencies can flag “unlawful” online content and directly trigger its takedown by internet platforms, all through a centralized interface.
Expansion of NATGRID: Perhaps the most far-reaching is the quiet expansion of NATGRID, India’s National Intelligence Grid. Long conceived as an integrated database for counter-terror investigations, NATGRID has recently morphed into a broad surveillance net. Following a high-level police conference in late November 2025, states were directed to “scale up” NATGRID usage beyond central agencies, even giving police officers at the Superintendent rank access to its vast datasets.
These developments match the increased use of AI technologies in domains of policing and welfare without a clear legal basis and real safeguards.

IFF acknowledges that the India AI Impact Summit 2026 offers a platform for dialogue and a chance for civil society voices to gain visibility on an international stage. We recognize the value in having digital rights perspectives included in global AI governance conversations, indeed, the Summit’s presence in India is an opportunity to spotlight our constitutional concerns before a world audience. We support our peer organizations and allies who choose to engage with the Summit, and we will remain in constructive collaboration with them. However, IFF has decided not to allocate significant organizational resources to direct participation in the Summit’s events. This is not a boycott of the forum, but a practical choice of focus. As a small team of only 7 full-time staff based in New Delhi, we must prioritize the most pressing advocacy initiatives that align closely with our mission and charter.

This includes ongoing efforts such as legal challenges to unconstitutional regulations, campaigning and community engagement for strengthening free expression, privacy and transparency frameworks. These are battles immediately affecting citizens’ rights and requiring our sustained attention. IFF will engage with the Summit in a mindful, critical manner. We will track the proceedings and outcomes closely, offering our analyses and critiques rooted in constitutional values. If and where we do participate (for example, in side events or discussions), we will do so with a critical gaze, centering the lived experiences of Indians and the paramountcy of our fundamental rights. Our support is firmly with the broader civil society coalition pushing for AI governance that is accountable and just.

India has quietly frozen Starlink. It issued the license nearly a year ago, then let the final security clearance sit, and the whole satellite-comms sector has slowed with it. This is not a compliance dispute. New Delhi is asking a question Starlink can't really answer: given its US ownership and global network, how can it promise to follow Indian rules when Washington wants the opposite?

What spooked them is concrete. Starlink terminals were used in the Iran war even though it holds no license in Iran. India watched a sovereign state fail to switch off a network running over its own territory, and asked who is next.

Notice the tell. Jio and Bharti get an easier ride because their satellite partners are European, not a US-controlled operator. The worry isn't the satellites, it's whose hand is on the switch. And it lands days before SpaceX's IPO at a $1.75tn valuation, with Starlink as the main revenue engine, a reminder that the global rollout is far from uniform: shut out of China, and now stuck in India too.

Free and Fearless Media 
Modi in 2014: “Democracy needs strong media that can stand against any big shot.”
2026: India 157/180 on press freedom. Neighbours above us.
2,312 blocks in one year. Then 1.95 lakh in five months. One order every 68 seconds. Two-hour deletion deadline.
Godi on TV. Delete button on the phone.
That’s not fearless media. That’s managed silencing.

Then Modi said this. Today India must ask why.

Listen carefully to the speaker in this video.

https://t.co/8SRxtaXoNG

It is Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

He says that in a democracy, the media must be strong. It must not run away. It must have the courage to stand up even to the most powerful people. A democracy, he says, cannot function without a fearless press. <FileCite ref_id=turn0file0/>

Those are not the words of an opposition leader.

They are Narendra Modi's own words.

And that is precisely why they deserve to be remembered today.

Because the real test of commitment to press freedom is not what a leader says before coming to power. It is what happens to journalism after that leader has held power for years.

Today, critics point to India's declining press-freedom rankings, growing pressure on independent journalists, concentration of media ownership, and increasing use of legal and administrative powers against media organisations and digital platforms. The debate is no longer whether the media should be fearless—Modi himself answered that question years ago.

The question is:

Has India moved closer to the fearless media Modi once called essential for democracy—or further away from it?

A free press is not one that praises the government.

A free press is one that can question the government without fear.

It can expose failures.

It can challenge lies.

It can hold every party accountable.

That was the standard Narendra Modi himself articulated.

Citizens are entitled to judge governments not only by their promises, but by their own words.

When leaders speak about democracy, history remembers the speech. Democracy remembers whether they lived by it.

Watch the video. These are the Prime Minister's own words.

#NarendraModi #PressFreedom #IndianDemocracy #FreeMedia #IndependentJournalism #Accountability #Truth

FREE SPEECH DOESN’T NEED A GOVERNMENT PERMISSION SLIP.

The Modi Government’s growing agenda for controlling what Indians can see, read, post, critique and challenge online should concern every citizen — regardless of political affiliation.

From demanding takedowns to tightening the time available to platforms to scrutinise government notices, the direction is unmistakable: comply first, question later. India’s 2026 IT-rule changes cut the takedown window for unlawful content to just three hours, while the Government has also proposed making certain official advisories legally binding on platforms. (Reuters⁠)

That is precisely why Elon Musk’s decision to resist, scrutinise and challenge government demands rather than blindly obey every request matters.

X’s own stated policy is that requests can be challenged when they are legally defective, overly broad or appear to impermissibly burden freedom of expression. (Transparency⁠)

And that is where the real problem begins for the Modi Government.

When an independent platform refuses to become an obedient extension of the State, the State’s attempts to control the narrative become visible.

No algorithm can hide that.
No press conference can spin that.
No amount of propaganda can erase that.

If the Government’s demands are genuinely about protecting citizens and enforcing legitimate law, let them withstand public scrutiny, judicial scrutiny and independent platform scrutiny.

But if criticism, dissent, inconvenient facts and uncomfortable questions are increasingly treated as “content to be removed”, then Musk’s resistance does something far more important than defending X.

It exposes this Govt’s vile intent and its surreptitious machinery.

And once the machinery is exposed, the Modi Government stands increasingly bare before the very citizens whose freedom of expression it claims to protect.

A democracy doesn’t become stronger by silencing criticism.
It becomes stronger by surviving it. 

There seems to be a crackdown on Modi Govt these days from every corner and every cross section of India. Are “Acche Din” finally around the corner for India ⁉️

2026: India 157/180 on press freedom. Neighbours above us.
2,312 blocks in one year. Then 1.95 lakh in five months. One order every 68 seconds. Two-hour deletion deadline.

A Student Spoke About an Unpaid Scholarship. The Journalist Reported It. Then Came the FIRs.

[Newslaundry — Khushi Mehrotra’s report]
https://t.co/4kxMks4eKh

What began as a student's complaint about an unpaid scholarship at COEP Technological University, Pune, has escalated into a political and legal battle involving rival student organisations, a campus confrontation and three FIRs—including one naming the journalist who reported the student's grievance. 

ABP Majha journalist Mandar Gonjari interviewed students at COEP ahead of Rahul Gandhi's Chhatron Ki Goonj programme. Among them was Sampada Pramod Bade, who said she had not received her scholarship for three years and had allegedly been charged fees under the general category despite being admitted under the orphan quota. Other students reportedly raised scholarship and hostel-related concerns as well. 

The report subsequently became politically useful to both sides. Congress's media cell circulated part of the report to challenge Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis's claim that students attending Gandhi's programme were from Congress-run institutions. 

Then the student's account changed.

Gonjari alleges that ABVP activists pressured Bade to retract her earlier statements, saying that the journalist had manipulated her and that her scholarship grievance was not genuine. Bade subsequently released a video saying that pressure had been created and that she had been manipulated. BJP also circulated another video in which she appealed for her campus to be freed from political activity. ABVP denies pressuring her. 

The dispute then escalated into an ABVP–NSUI confrontation on August 21.

Three FIRs followed:

An ABVP complaint alleged assault and pressure on the student by NSUI/Congress workers.

A Youth Congress complaint alleged that Bade was confined in the hostel and that Congress workers were assaulted.

A COEP administration complaint alleged trespassing by NSUI/Congress workers and also named journalist Mandar Gonjari over alleged unauthorised entry. 

There is an important distinction here: the FIR does not allege that Gonjari participated in the alleged violence or sloganeering. Gonjari denies entering the hostel and says the interviews were recorded in an open area near the college canteen, in daylight, with other journalists and security personnel present. The police say the matter is under investigation. 

The Pune Union of Working Journalists has condemned the journalist's inclusion and asked the police commissioner to remove him from the case. 

There is also an important unresolved question about the scholarship itself. A Youth Congress representative told Newslaundry that the scholarship money was released after the ABP Majha report went viral—but that claim comes from the political representative and should not be presented as independently established fact without further documentation. COEP itself confirms that it administers numerous government and other scholarships. 

The fundamental issue

A student raises a legitimate grievance.

A journalist investigates and reports it.

Political organisations then contest the narrative.

A campus confrontation follows.

And suddenly the journalist himself becomes a criminal accused.

That should concern everyone who believes in a free press.

Journalists must of course be accountable if they actually trespass, fabricate evidence or participate in violence. But those allegations must be established through evidence—not manufactured through political pressure.

The police must therefore investigate all sides impartially:

Was the student's original scholarship grievance genuine?
Why did her account subsequently change?
Was she pressured by anyone?
What does the CCTV footage show?
Where exactly was the journalist when he conducted the interview?
Did he enter the hostel at all?
Who initiated the campus violence?
And why ...Cont'd

The @DoT_India notified the Telecommunications (User Identification) Rules, 2026 (“the Rules”) on 21 August 2026. The Rules mandate that telecom operators verify the facial biometric information of every person who chooses to obtain a new SIM, replace or change their details, or even surrender their number. 

(1/n)
#privacy #surveillance #biometric

It seems that the Rules, along with the circular, aim to revive the same mandates that have been struck down as illegal and unconstitutional by the Supreme Court in the past.

(9/n)
#privacy #surveillance #biometric

Such measures present a grave threat to the fundamental right to privacy for millions of Indians, as it requires private entities to collect and process troves of biometric information based on justifications that fail to satisfy the test of proportionality and necessity.

(10/n)
#privacy #surveillance #biometric

This live biometric verification process may involve the collection and processing of sensitive personal information like your face, fingerprint or iris.

(2/n)
#privacy #surveillance #biometric

Along with the Rules, the DoT has issued a circular to operationalise the Digital Intelligence Platform (“DIP”). The platform will share a “representative image” of each user with telecom operators every day to enforce the nine-SIM limit and prevent users from getting additional connections.

(3/n)
#privacy #surveillance #biometric

https://t.co/fQcMLwYL9X, a crowdsourced platform created to anonymously document alleged demands for bribes has been temporarily taken offline, citing concerns around traffic, data security, spam, duplicate entries, and misuse.

The public disclosure of alleged demands has also raised questions about the criminal liability of complainants. Under the Prevention of Corruption Act, bribing a public servant is punishable with up to seven years’ imprisonment. Those who report the demand within seven days are exempt from punishment. However, a public disclosure on a website falls outside that protection.

Speaking to @timesofindia, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 founder @mishichoudhary highlights the importance of data minimisation, security by design, and anonymity on such platforms to protect complainants' identities.

text:
A 2.6 million-view Instagram reel documenting the concerns of residents affected by a proposed Google data centre in Visakhapatnam was blocked in India without prior notice, a hearing, or a copy of the blocking order being provided to the journalists who made it. When the order was finally obtained through litigation, it referred to an entirely unrelated individual. IFF has now sought a review and restoration of the reel.
Read More: https://t.co/z4Ps7Umqrk

The blocking order itself raised serious concerns. It referred to a person named Mr. Vemireddy Prabhakar Reddy, who is entirely unknown to the journalists and has no connection whatsoever with the reel, which featured interviews with residents of Tarluvada village. The journalists were also never given an opportunity to respond or defend their reporting. (6/7)

IFF has now issued a legal notice seeking a periodic review of the blocking under the IT Rules, 2021, a proper hearing for the journalists, disclosure of the grounds for the restriction, and restoration of the reel. A factual ground report affecting freedom of speech and journalistic work cannot be restricted through an opaque process without procedural safeguards. (7/7)

text:
A Delhi High Court order has once again had to remind the Grievance Appellate Committee to follow the timeline already prescribed under the IT Rules, 2021. On 20 August 2026, the Court directed the GAC to decide the appeal of content creator Riya, whose Instagram account #riaspeaks has over five lakh followers, within 30 days. Her appeal had already been pending for more than 42 days. (1/7)
Read More: https://t.co/26gA6SeMe0

The GAC is particularly important because it is supposed to provide users with an appellate remedy against intermediary decisions, including arbitrary or permanent account bans. Yet when an appeal itself remains pending beyond the prescribed period, a creator can be left with no meaningful remedy except approaching a High Court. The burden then falls on users and the judiciary alike. (6/7)

IFF had earlier suggested increasing the number of GACs to deal with the growing volume of appeals and making GAC orders publicly accessible, given the quasi-adjudicatory nature of their work. Neither has happened. We are assisting Riya through the appeal process and will continue to monitor the matter. (7/7)
